title: The Most Famous Brothers in Football History | WinFulltime
description: The Toures, Charltons, Laudrups, Nevilles and more. Meet the most famous brothers in football history and the trophies they won together.
keywords: famous brothers football, brother footballers, Kolo and Yaya Toure, Charlton brothers, Neville brothers, Hazard brothers, football siblings
h1: The Most Famous Brothers in Football History
lead: Football runs in families, but some families have produced pairs of genuine superstars. These are the most famous brothers in football history — and the dynasties they built.
thumbCaption: The most famous brothers in football history
share: Toure, Charlton, Laudrup, Neville, Hazard — the greatest brother acts football has ever seen.
content:
Every great player is one of a kind. Some of them are not. Football history is full of brothers who reached the top together, and a handful of pairs are among the greatest players of their era at the same time. These are the most famous brothers in football history.

Kolo and Yaya Toure

No modern pair defined their era like the Toure brothers from Ivory Coast. Kolo Toure was the bedrock of Arsenal's famous 'Invincibles' back line in 2003-04, then won more silverware at Manchester City. Yaya Toure was the dominant box-to-box midfielder of the 2010s, winning three Premier League titles, an FA Cup and the Champions League with Barcelona, and being named African Footballer of the Year four times. Together they anchored the Ivory Coast team for a decade.

Bobby and Jack Charlton

England's 1966 World Cup winners featured two brothers: Bobby Charlton, the free-scoring midfield genius of Manchester United, and Jack Charlton, the towering centre-back. They remain the only brothers to start and win a World Cup final for England. Their paths could hardly have differed more — Bobby was the silky attacker, Jack the rugged defender — but the medal was shared.

Michael and Brian Laudrup

Denmark's Euro 1992 fairy tale was powered by two brothers. Michael Laudrup was one of the most gifted playmakers of the 1980s and 90s, winning La Liga with Barcelona and Real Madrid. Brian Laudrup was the electrifying winger who scored in the 1992 final against Germany and won the Champions League with Rangers' rivals AC Milan. Their father Finn had also played for Denmark, making the Laudrups a genuine dynasty.

Ronald and Erwin Koeman

Netherlands' Euro 1988 winners included two Koeman brothers. Ronald Koeman — who later managed Barcelona — was the free-kick specialist whose goals included the famous penalty that beat West Germany in the semi-final, while Erwin Koeman was a tenacious midfielder. Ronald's trophy haul stretched from PSV to Barcelona, including the 1992 European Cup.

Gary and Phil Neville

The Neville brothers were the perfect example of academy loyalty. Both came through Manchester United's youth system, won the treble in 1999, and won a combined 19 Premier League titles. Gary was the relentless right-back and later captain; Phil played both full-back and midfield. Together they won more than almost any sibling pairing in English football.

Eden and Thorgan Hazard

Belgium's golden generation featured the Hazard brothers. Eden Hazard was the Premier League's most feared dribbler at Chelsea, twice winning the title, while Thorgan Hazard built a fine career in the Bundesliga at Borussia Monchengladbach and later at Dortmund. A third brother, Kylian, also played professionally. They formed the spine of Belgium's second-ranked national team of the late 2010s.

Lucas and Theo Hernandez

The Hernandez brothers from France each won football's biggest prize. Lucas Hernandez won the 2018 World Cup with France and the Champions League with Bayern Munich. His younger brother Theo Hernandez has been AC Milan's attacking left-back since 2019, and starred for France at the 2022 World Cup. It is rare for two brothers from the same family to reach the top of the European game, let alone the World Cup final.

The Boateng Brothers and the Williams Siblings

Two more modern pairs deserve a mention. Kevin-Prince and Jerome Boateng are half-brothers who played on opposite international sides: Kevin-Prince for Ghana, Jerome for Germany, where he won the 2014 World Cup. And the Williams brothers, Iñaki and Nico, starred for Spain at Euro 2024, with Nico scoring in the final as Spain won the title.

title: Famous Father-and-Son Footballers | WinFulltime
description: The Maldinis, Schmeichels, Haalands and Cruyffs. The most famous father-and-son footballers who both played the game at the highest level.
keywords: father son footballers, footballer father son, Maldini father son, Schmeichel father son, Haaland father son, football dynasties father son
lead: Some footballers become their father's legacy. These famous father-and-son pairs both reached the professional game — and several both won major trophies.
share: Maldini, Schmeichel, Haaland, Hagi — the fathers and sons who both reached the top of football.
content:
Handing a shirt down from father to son is one of football's most romantic stories. The names are familiar to fans of several generations: a surname heard in the terraces as a legend, then heard again twenty years later for his son. These are the most famous father-and-son footballers in the history of the game.

Cesare and Paolo Maldini

The ultimate father-son story belongs to AC Milan. Cesare Maldini captained Milan and won the 1963 European Cup, then became a respected coach and Italy manager. His son Paolo Maldini went further, spending his entire 24-year career at Milan, winning five European Cups and seven Serie A titles, and captaining Italy at the 1994 World Cup final. No family name is more woven into a single club.

Peter and Kasper Schmeichel

Football's only father-son Premier League-winning goalkeepers. Peter Schmeichel won five Premier League titles with Manchester United and the 1999 treble. His son Kasper Schmeichel followed a far harder road — released from Manchester City, rebuilt at Notts County and Leeds — before winning the Premier League with Leicester City in 2016 and the FA Cup in 2021, plus the Euro 2020 run to the semi-finals with Denmark.

Frank Lampard Senior and Junior

Frank Lampard Sr won two FA Cups and 552 appearances for West Ham. His son Frank Lampard Jr became Chelsea's all-time top scorer with 211 goals, won three Premier League titles and the 2012 Champions League, and holds the Premier League record for goals from midfield. Theirs is a rare case where the son was even better than the father.

Johan and Jordi Cruyff

Johan Cruyff reinvented football as a player and coach, winning three European Cups and three Ballons d'Or. His son Jordi Cruyff was a fine winger in his own right, playing for Barcelona and Manchester United and winning Euro 1996 qualification-era caps for the Netherlands. Jordi later followed his father into management and worked at Barcelona and as a national team coach.

Gheorghe and Ianis Hagi

Gheorghe Hagi, the 'Maradona of the Carpathians', is Romania's greatest-ever player. His son Ianis Hagi became a professional and represented Romania, following his father's footsteps. It is a rare international father-son pairing, with Ianis playing alongside the national record-holder who shares his name.

George and Timothy Weah

George Weah was the first African footballer to win the Ballon d'Or and later became president of Liberia. His son Timothy Weah chose to play for the United States, won Ligue 1 with Lille, and started for the USMNT at the 2022 World Cup. A Ballon d'Or-winning father and a World Cup son — few families come close.

Alfie and Erling Haaland

Alfie Haaland played for Leeds, Nottingham Forest and Manchester City in the Premier League. His son Erling Haaland has rewritten the goalscoring record books — 36 Premier League goals in his debut season, and a 2023 treble with Manchester City. Father and son both played at Elland Road and for Norway, and Erling has often credited Alfie's coaching for his finishing.

Diego and Giovanni Simeone

Atletico Madrid's long-time manager Diego Simeone was one of Argentina's great midfielders. His eldest son Giovanni Simeone became a Serie A striker of note, scoring regularly for several Italian clubs and winning caps for Argentina. The Simeone name now spans two generations of the professional game.

The rarest record: Only the Schmeichels have both won the Premier League. Only the Maldinis have captained the same club to a European Cup. Father-son footballers are common; father-son winners are precious.

h1: The Greatest Football Families in History
lead: One great player is talent. Two is coincidence. Three is a football family. These are the dynasties whose bloodlines produced generation after generation of professionals.
thumbCaption: The greatest football families in history
share: From the three-generation Maldinis to the Charlton brothers, these are football's greatest family dynasties.
content:
Scouting departments spend fortunes searching for the next generation of talent. Some families simply produce it. Across the history of the game, a handful of names have kept coming back: brothers, sons, cousins and even grandchildren, all of them professional footballers, several of them among the best of their era.

The Maldini Dynasty

No family is more deeply embedded in one club than the Maldinis of AC Milan. Cesare Maldini was the captain who lifted the 1963 European Cup. His son Paolo played 902 matches for Milan and won five European Cups. And when Daniel Maldini debuted for Milan in 2021, he became the third generation to play for the club his grandfather and father had captained. Three generations, one shirt, one city.

The Laudrups: A Danish Football Royalty

Denmark's greatest footballing family began with Finn Laudrup, a winger capped for Denmark in the 1960s and 70s. His sons Michael and Brian became two of the greatest Danish players ever, winning Euro 1992, and Michael went on to win La Liga with both Barcelona and Real Madrid. Three internationals from one family, across two generations, is rare enough — the Laudrups made it look easy.

The Cruyffs

Johan Cruyff is the most influential figure in the sport's modern history — a three-time Ballon d'Or winner and the tactical father of Total Football. His son Jordi played for Barcelona and Manchester United and later became a coach, carrying the philosophy on. The Cruyff influence extends beyond bloodlines into the very DNA of Barcelona's style of play.

The Toures and the Charltons

Two brother pairs above all others define sibling excellence in football. The Charlton brothers, Bobby and Jack, won the 1966 World Cup together and remain the only brothers to do so for England. The Toure brothers, Kolo and Yaya, were the backbone of both the Arsenal Invincibles and the rise of Manchester City, winning Premier League titles in the same era.

The Benders: Germany's Identical Duo

Lars and Sven Bender were identical twins who both became German internationals. Lars won the Bundesliga with Borussia Dortmund in the 2011-12 double season, while Sven built his career at Bayer Leverkusen. Two twins, two international caps, one family — a genuinely unusual footballing story.

The Simeones: From Cholo to Giovanni

Diego Simeone was Argentina's combative midfield general and is now one of Europe's most successful managers. His son Giovanni became a Serie A striker, and a second son, Gianluca, also plays professional football. The Simeones are one of the few families with two generations of top-level players and one generation managing at the very top.

The Boateng Brothers

Jerome Boateng won the 2014 World Cup with Germany and the treble with Bayern Munich. His older half-brother Kevin-Prince Boateng played for Ghana and had a remarkable European career spanning Tottenham, AC Milan and Barcelona. Brothers on opposite international sides, both world class in their positions, is a story unique to the Boateng name.

title: Footballers With Unusual Pre-Match Rituals | WinFulltime
description: Bruce Grobbelaar's spaghetti legs, Peter Schmeichel's star jump, Ronaldo's sock routine. The strangest behavioural pre-match rituals in football.
keywords: footballers pre match rituals, pre match routines, Grobbelaar spaghetti legs, Schmeichel star jump, Ronaldo pre match routine, football warm up routines
lead: Before the whistle blows, some of the world's best players do things that make no sense at all. These are the behavioural pre-match rituals footballers repeat before every single match.
thumbCaption: The strangest pre-match rituals in football
share: Spaghetti legs, star jumps and meditating strikers — the strangest pre-match rituals in football history.
content:
Footballers are famously creatures of habit. Before a match, many perform the same warm-up, wear the same equipment and follow the same sequence of actions they have used for years. Most of these routines are sensible preparation. A few are bizarre enough to become part of football folklore.

What Rituals Actually Do

Psychologists call pre-match routines 'control behaviours'. They give a player a familiar sequence in an unfamiliar situation, reducing anxiety and providing a sense of order before ninety minutes of chaos. The ritual itself rarely matters — the confidence it provides does.

Bruce Grobbelaar's Spaghetti Legs

The most famous pre-kickoff routine in football history belongs to Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar. During the 1984 European Cup final penalty shootout against Roma, with the entire match on the line, Grobbelaar wobbled his legs like spaghetti and did a jig on his goal line between kicks. The antics unsettled the Roma takers, Liverpool won the shootout, and 'spaghetti legs' entered football legend. He did it again at the 1990 FA Cup final, earning Liverpool the trophy once more.

Jerzy Dudek's Homage

Grobbelaar's routine was so famous that it was deliberately copied. In the 2005 Champions League final, Liverpool's Jerzy Dudek recreated the spaghetti-legs wobble before Milan's final penalty. It worked: Andriy Shevchenko missed, and Liverpool completed the greatest comeback in Champions League history.

Peter Schmeichel's Star Jump

Before facing penalties, Manchester United's Peter Schmeichel would spread his arms and legs wide in a 'star jump' and hold the pose as the taker ran up — a routine he brought from his handball background. The physical expansion made him look twice his size and is still studied by goalkeeping coaches today.

Roberto Baggio's Meditation

The Italian maestro Roberto Baggio, a practising Buddhist, meditated before matches. He would retreat into quiet focus before big games, using a routine that the Italian national team's psychologists encouraged. In an era of screaming managers, a striker who prepared by going quiet was as unusual as it was effective.

Antonio Rüdiger's Pre-Match Sprint

One of the most recognisable modern routines belongs to Antonio Rüdiger. Before kickoff, the Germany and Real Madrid defender sprints down the touchline, screams and shakes his head violently, working himself into a state of high arousal before the game begins. Fans have turned it into a meme, but the routine serves a real purpose: Rüdiger says it gets his body ready for the physical intensity of the match.

The Ronaldo Sock and Boot Routine

Cristiano Ronaldo is famous for his preparation. He reportedly follows the same dressing-room sequence before every match — his socks rolled to the same height, his shin pads in the same position, his boots laced in the same way — and refuses to let anyone else touch his match boots. Whether it is superstition or habit, the routine has accompanied a two-decade career at the absolute top.

The Goalkeeper's Crossbar Touch

Watch any big game and you will see goalkeepers touch the crossbar before kickoff, often with both hands. It is one of the most widespread behavioural rituals in sport: a physical check that the goal is solid, a mental reset, and a claiming of the space they will defend for the next ninety minutes.

The common thread: Every one of these routines — from spaghetti legs to a quiet meditation — puts the player in control of something before a game they cannot control. That is the entire point.

title: The Strangest Superstitions in Football History | WinFulltime
description: Blanc kissing Barthez's head, the centre-circle taboo and lucky kits. The strangest superstitions in football history, explained.
keywords: strangest football superstitions, football superstitions, Blanc Barthez head kiss, lucky boots football, football lucky rituals, centre circle superstition
h1: The Strangest Superstitions in Football History
lead: Lucky socks, forbidden grass, a goalkeeper whose head had to be kissed. Football is full of superstition — these are the strangest beliefs the game has ever seen.
thumbCaption: The strangest superstitions in football history
share: From Blanc kissing Barthez's head to the centre-circle taboo — football's strangest superstitions.
content:
Professional footballers are rational, disciplined, highly paid athletes. They are also, apparently, deeply superstitious. Ask a squad about their pre-match habits and half of them will admit to a lucky object, a lucky routine or a thing they simply refuse to do. This guide is about those beliefs — the objects and taboos — rather than matchday meals, which we have covered separately.

Laurent Blanc and Fabien Barthez's Lucky Head

The most famous superstition in modern international football involved two Frenchmen. Before France's matches in the 1998 World Cup and Euro 2000, defender Laurent Blanc would walk over to goalkeeper Fabien Barthez and kiss his shaved head — a ritual the team became convinced brought them luck. France won both tournaments, and when Blanc was suspended for the 1998 semi-final and could not perform the ritual, the nation held its breath. The superstition had become so famous that it defined the team's identity.

Ronaldo's Pre-Final Haircut

Before the 2002 World Cup final, Brazil's Ronaldo turned up with a bizarre half-shaved haircut that made headlines worldwide. His explanation was revealing: he had cut it deliberately to shift the media attention away from his team-mates and onto himself. The superstition-adjacent logic worked — Brazil won the final 2-0 and Ronaldo scored both goals, proving that even the pre-match rituals of superstars can be engineered for effect.

The Centre-Circle Taboo

Ask players about one of the game's quietest superstitions and many will mention the centre circle. A surprising number of players — particularly strikers and attacking midfielders — refuse to step on or touch the halfway line during the warm-up, treating it as a boundary that crossing brings bad luck. There is no official record of where this belief began, but it persists across dressing rooms to this day.

Lucky Kits and Unbeaten Runs

Clubs are as superstitious as individuals. When a team is on an unbeaten run, managers routinely refuse to change anything — the same kit, the same dressing-room allocation, even the same pre-match schedule. The most famous example is Ajax's 26-match winning run in 1971-72, where the club kept everything identical to avoid 'breaking the spell'. For the full history of such streaks, see our guide to the longest winning streaks in football.

The Goalkeeper's Lucky Goal

Goalkeepers have their own superstitions around the goal. Many refuse to touch the net before kickoff, others will not let anyone but themselves hang their gloves on the post, and a well-documented minority insist on stepping onto the pitch with the same foot first. Even the great Dino Zoff, Italy's 1982 World Cup-winning keeper, admitted to a pre-match ritual of walking to his goal in exactly the same way.

Worn-In Boots and Unbroken Habits

Perhaps the most common superstition in football is the lucky boot. Players who score on debut often wear the same pair until the streak ends, and some refuse to change boots at half-time even when soaked. Cristiano Ronaldo's refusal to let anyone handle his match boots is the modern, heavily documented version of the same belief: the equipment that brought success must be protected.

The Fan Superstitions

Superstition is not confined to the pitch. The Iceland supporters' famous 'thunderclap' was originally a ritual designed to will their team forward, and fans around the world have their own beliefs — from lucky scarves to the tradition of never sitting in someone else's seat. Even the 'curse' stories that cling to certain stadiums and trophies are superstitions, told with a straight face by otherwise rational people.

The psychology: Superstitions work because they give players a feeling of control over outcomes that are largely random. A striker who believes his boots are lucky steps onto the pitch more confident — and confidence is genuinely valuable.
